questions.text: Who asked the question "Can machines think?" in 1950, laying the foundation for the field of AI?

options.text: The team that built ELIZA at MIT

questions.explanation: The story begins in 1950 with mathematician Alan Turing, whose philosophical question gave researchers a direction that would drive decades of work.

questions.text: The lesson describes the progress of AI over the past seventy years as steady and linear.
questions.explanation: The lesson says the opposite: progress has never been linear, moving in waves of excitement and disappointment, including two periods known as AI winters.

questions.text: Which of these statements match the timeline given in the lesson?

options.text: IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997.
ELIZA was created at MIT in 1966 and mimicked a psychotherapist.
The Transformer architecture was invented in 2017.
ChatGPT was released to the public in 2016.
The first AI winter came because symbolic systems had become too accurate to keep funding.

questions.explanation: Deep Blue (1997), ELIZA (1966) and the Transformer (2017) all appear in the timeline; ChatGPT was released in November 2022, and the first winter came because early systems failed to scale beyond toy problems.

questions.text: According to the lesson, what makes the last few years a genuine turning point for education?

options.text: AI finally passed the Turing Test under laboratory conditions.
AI became accessible — teachers can use it by simply typing a question in natural language.
Governments made AI training mandatory for teachers.
AI became cheap enough for schools to run on their own servers.

questions.explanation: The lesson's key insight is that the real revolution is not just that AI got better, but that it became accessible — usable without programming knowledge, which turned it from an abstract concept into an everyday tool.
